body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.
The Victorian Liberals are today dealing with the fallout of being forced to dump Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann over offensive social media posts.

Independent candidate says Williamstown race has opened up
An independent candidate for the electorate where a Liberal candidate was disendorsed by his party says the campaign for the seat has become "very dynamic".
Yesterday, the Liberals dumped Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann over offensive views he expressed about Indigenous Australians that had recently come to light.
It's left the party without a candidate to contest the seat, currently held by Labor MP Melissa Horne.
Speaking on 774 ABC Melbourne, West Party candidate Gill Gannon says her community is looking for change.

"I'm not sure how it's all going to play out, we're in a very, very dynamic situation … at the moment," she said. "I think there's an appetite for change in our electorate and we're hoping that that happens."
"I'm not sure how it's all going to play out, we're in a very, very dynamic situation … at the moment," she said.
"I think there's an appetite for change in our electorate and we're hoping that that happens."
Mr Lindemann has been contacted for comment.
Key policy in focus: The VCAA
Last night, visitors to the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA) website were greeted with an expletive-riddled message.

A hacker, who signed off as "DaggerElite", claimed they had downloaded a copy of the 2026 exam papers from the printing provider's internal file servers and distributed copies using email details obtained from the legal service provider.
But VCAA chief executive Andrew Smith said this morning the hacker had not accessed exam papers.

"We've worked overnight; there is no evidence that these exams have been leaked," he told 774 ABC Melbourne. "The arrangements that are in place to secure them are well established arrangements, they're very stringent."
"We've worked overnight; there is no evidence that these exams have been leaked," he told 774 ABC Melbourne.
"The arrangements that are in place to secure them are well established arrangements, they're very stringent."
It's the latest in a string of controversies for the embattled agency, which has overseen repeated blunders on exams in recent years.
In 2022 and 2023, errors were identified in mathematics exams, with the VCAA forced to apologise to students.
In 2024, a blunder allowed students sitting the VCE exams to access questions online ahead of time that were the same or similar to those that appeared on the actual tests.
Cover sheets in sample exams for some subjects contained questions in transparent text that could be revealed if copied and pasted into another document.
The blunder led to then-education minister Ben Carroll sacking the entire VCAA board in 2025, and the government vowed to improve the VCAA following an investigation.
By coincidence, the shadow education minister at the time was Jess Wilson, who was fiercely critical of Carroll's handling of the issue.
Labor committed $222.2 million in the 2026/27 budget to reform the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority.
But it remains to be seen how any future government will handle the VCAA after the coming election.
Seats in focus: Bulleen

Bulleen has been held by the Liberal Party for its entire existence, and has mostly been a safe seat. But in recent years, its margin has fallen to around 5 per cent on a two-candidate preferred basis. This may be in part due to the Liberals’ declining reputation among the Chinese Australians who make up around 30 per cent of the seat's population, mostly due to damaging remarks by federal Liberals.

The seat’s incumbent MP is Matthew Guy, who led the Liberals into the 2018 and 2022 elections. He was preceded by Nick Kotsiras, who was multicultural affairs minister in the Baillieu government and is himself a Greek Australian, with people of Greek heritage also a significant community in the seat. Kotsiras was elected in 1999 after defeating incumbent Liberal MP David Perrin in a preselection battle. Perrin was a backbencher during Jeff Kennett’s time in government and often advocated for more conservative positions.

Despite the falling Liberal margin over time, the opposition would still be favoured to hold this seat given Labor’s difficulties in retaining government. While the seat leans conservative, its cultural diversity means it would not be one of One Nation’s best chances at this election.
Greens leader tells other parties to 'grow up' and debate
As mentioned by Richard Willingham in his analysis this morning, the ABC debate will not go ahead after the Liberals declined the invitation.
A separate debate proposed by Nine has also been scrapped after Labor turned it down.
Now, Greens leader Ellen Sandell has blasted the major parties over their decisions

"If you want to lead Victoria, if you want people to vote for you, you should be able to get through an hour of questions without weeks of negotiations about who’s allowed in the room — and you should be prepared to do that where everyone can watch for free. It’s no wonder people are fed up with the major parties," Sandell said.
Sandell said avoiding a televised debate showed the other three parties invited were "completely devoid of any vision for Victoria".

"While it’s disappointing that they won’t show up for Victorians, it’s not all that surprising because none of these parties have plans that pass the pub test," she said. "We said yes to the ABC. There’s still time for all four leaders to show up, so I say grow up."
"While it’s disappointing that they won’t show up for Victorians, it’s not all that surprising because none of these parties have plans that pass the pub test," she said.
"We said yes to the ABC. There’s still time for all four leaders to show up, so I say grow up."
Why the ABC and other media are not hosting Victorian election debates in 2026

We're told by our political leaders that this is the most consequential election in the state's history, yet getting Premier Ben Carroll and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson to debate is proving difficult.
Wilson turned down an invitation for a debate hosted by the ABC, while Carroll turned down a similar invitation from the Nine group.
Behind the scenes, parties insist that voters aren't interested in debates.
The result is an ever more controlled and scripted election, playing out on social media.

Key Event
Jess Wilson 'disappointed' over Liberals candidate vetting
Liberal leader Jess Wilson says it's disappointing her party was not aware of offensive comments made by one of its candidates.
Yesterday, the party dumped Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann, over views he expressed on social media about Indigenous Australians that had recently come to light.
Appearing on the ABC's News Breakfast program this morning, Wilson said the comments made by Lindemann were deeply offensive.
"I have the highest of standards when it comes to my team and we acted swiftly to disendorse," she said. "It's disappointing that the vetting process did not show this up."
"I have the highest of standards when it comes to my team and we acted swiftly to disendorse," she said.
"It's disappointing that the vetting process did not show this up."
Key Event
Liberal candidate for Williamstown dumped over offensive comments
The Victorian Liberal Party has dumped Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann over offensive comments it says he made about Indigenous Australians.
In a statement, the party says it has withdrawn its support and endorsement of Lindemann over views he expressed, which had recently come to light.

"These comments are offensive, unacceptable and inconsistent with the values and standards expected of Liberal candidates," the statement says. "All candidates are expected to treat Australians with dignity and respect. Mr Lindemann's comments fell short of that standard."

The party was not previously aware of Lindemann's comments, the statement says.
The ABC has attempted to contact Lindemann for comment.
Welcome to the live blog
We're bringing you live coverage today from the Victorian state election campaign trail.
After a brief pause for Remembrance Day, Labor and the Liberals will resume their election campaigns, travelling across the state in big campaign buses to visit critical electorates.
